lines.text: A typesetting system takes a description of a document and decides where
every character goes. It breaks paragraphs into lines, stacks the lines into pages
and places headings, notes and figures where the reader expects them. Each of
these steps follows rules that can be written down precisely, and a good program
follows them exactly.
Lines of a paragraph are chosen together rather than one at a time.
The program looks at every way of breaking the paragraph and
picks the one whose lines are spaced most evenly, avoiding hyphens
on consecutive lines and very loose lines next to very tight ones.
Pages are built one line at a time. As each line arrives the program measures
how well the page would look if it ended there, and when adding more would
only make it worse it stops and starts a new page. Penalties discourage breaks
in awkward places, such as after the first line of a paragraph or before its last.
Vertical space between paragraphs and around headings can stretch
and shrink a little, so that a page whose lines do not exactly fill it
can still be set with its last line at the bottom. The amount of
stretch is small, and most of it goes where a reader will not notice.
Notes at the foot of a page are collected separately from the main
text. They take space from the page they appear on, and when there
are too many some of them move to the next page, keeping their
order and their numbers.
